title: Judge finds RCMP justified in fatal Fort McMurray gunfight
subtitle: A public inquiry into a fatal police shooting has found that RCMP officers acted appropriately when they shot and killed Ahmad Abdallah during a gunfight in a Fort McMurray apartment building in March 2011. "In my view, the officers involved in this incident did precisely what they should have done under the circumstances," wrote Provincial Court Judge Jim Jacques in a report released on Thursday.
article: A public inquiry into a fatal police shooting has found that RCMP officers acted appropriately when they shot and killed Ahmad Abdallah during a gunfight in a Fort McMurray apartment building in March 2011.
"In my view, the officers involved in this incident did precisely what they should have done under the circumstances," wrote Provincial Court Judge Jim Jacques in a report released on Thursday.
At the time of the shooting, the 24-year-old Abdallah was drunk, high on methamphetamine and armed with a loaded 9mm Glock handgun.

The shooting took place early on March 16, 2011, after Abdallah pulled out the gun after being asked to remove his shoes while visiting an apartment in Fort McMurray. One of the people in the apartment locked herself in the bathroom and called 911, and Abdallah then shot the gun into the floor twice while she was on the phone with emergency operators.

Jacques said police were at the scene within minutes, and arrived knowing shots had already been fired. The five officers entered the building immediately, after one broke the glass door with the butt off a shotgun.

Jacques said the officers were approaching the apartment when Abdallah shot at one officer, who then returned fire with his shotgun, hitting Abdallah once in the side. Abdallah then fired again, hitting another officer in the leg. That officer was injured but was able to shoot back, hitting Abdallah in the back.
Jacques report said both of the gunshot wounds Abdallah received "would have been rapidly fatal."
One of Abdallah's bullets was later found lodged in the first officer's radio, and Jacques' report noted that if it weren't for the radio, that officer would likely also have been hit.
Another shot fired by Abdallah didn't hit anyone, but was found inside a neighbouring apartment, which was vacant at the time. He had four more bullets in his gun when he died.
Jacques concluded the officers who shot Abdallah "responded promptly, intelligently and bravely to a potentially life-threatening situation."
"It is not unlikely that (the officers) saved not only their own lives, but those of their fellow officers by reacting rapidly and accurately to a deadly threat," he wrote.
The RCMP officers at the scene were identified in the report only by their last names, as constables Marshall, Curnew, Murray, Gibson and Doe.

RCMP spokeswoman Josee Valiquette refused to provide the officers' first names, saying "there's no need to further bring attention" to them. A spokesperson for Justice and Solicitor General, which released the report, said the government won't release the officers' first names either, and is leaving it up to the RCMP.
The report identified Marshall and Curnew as the officers directly involved in the shooting, and Curnew as the officer who was shot. She had been on the force 10 months at the time of the shooting.
Valiquette said she did not know whether the officers involved in the shooting are still with the RCMP, but later confirmed Curnew is no longer with the police force.

A 2012 investigation by Alberta Serious Incident Response Team also concluded that the shooting had been justified, finding that "both police officers were acting lawfully and in self-defence when they fired their weapons."

A public fatality inquiry examines the circumstances around a death, and makes recommendations about how to avoid similar deaths in the future. Based on his finding that officers actions acted appropriately in the situation, Jacques said he had no recommendations.
Valiquette said RCMP's "thought are with the Abdallah's family and all those impacted by his death."
"No police officer ever wants to be in a position where they have to shoot somebody, unfortunately that possibility is a reality of life on the front line," she said.
